Government Communications Security Bureau—Inquiry into Unlawful
Interception of Communications
10. CHARLES CHAUVEL (Labour)  to the Prime Minister : When will he be
informed of the Inspector-General’s findings concerning the three cases where the
24 Oct 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6125
Government Communications Security Bureau has been unable to assure him that its
actions have been lawful, and how will he communicate those findings to the House?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I expect to be informed of the inspector-
general’s findings when his review of the case is complete. Any decisions regarding the
communication of those findings will be made  then. However, I would note that my
own public statement on 3 Oct ober said that the Governme nt Communications Security
Bureau would issue a further public statement when legal work has been concluded.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: Will he ensure that the New Zealanders who were the subject of
the surveillance will be informed if it is  found that the surveillance of them was
unlawful; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I cannot guarantee that. I would have to take advice on
whether that is a sensible course of action to follow.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: When he told the Leader of th e Opposition last Tuesday that he
had seen the paperwork on which the bureau relied to support its belief that it had “acted
legally” in conducting surveillance on Mr Do tcom and his associates, and that this
material had formed the basis of the bureau’s  request to the Acting Prime Minister for a
ministerial certificate, what was the nature of that paperwork?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Possibly the way I should have phrased that is “some of the
paperwork”. I am sure there is more pape rwork that the Govern ment Communications
Security Bureau has. But, amongst other th ings, I have seen email correspondence from
the legal team at the bureau that supports the view that Mr Dotcom was not protected.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: Is he now satisfied that the co rrespondence to which he has just
referred was incorrect in substance?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think by nature we admitted that was the case, because that
was the view formed by the Government Comm unications Security Bureau’s legal team
after it did the review in the middle of Februa ry of this year. But,  of course, later on,
after the affidavit was signed, it was presen ted to the court by Paul Davison QC on
behalf of Kim Dotcom on 7 September 2012. A further review was undertaken, and it
was at that point, some time after that, that the bureau formed the vi ew that it had, in
fact, applied the wrong legal interpretation at that point.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: Is it normal practice for him not  be informed promptly by the
Government Communications Security Bureau or by his deputy that  in his absence the
bureau has sought, and his deputy has granted, a ministerial certificate to prevent a court
from considering the bureau’s activities in a particular court case?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I could not possibly ask for in formation on something that I
was not aware was taking place. I think I have said in this House a number of weeks ago
that, in fact, the failing, I think, was on the Government Comm unications Security
Bureau not to have informed me that it ha d asked the Minister to sign a ministerial
certificate. I might add, though, th at had I seen all of the information that the Acting
Prime Minister saw, without doubt and without hesitation I would have signed the same
documentation.
Child Health Services—Free After-hours Medical Care for Under-sixes for
Accidental Injuries
11. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister for ACC : How will the
Government improve accidental injury outcomes for under-six-year-olds?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I am very pleased  to announce that
free after-hours doctors’ visits  for under-6-year-olds will be  extended to visits covered
by ACC. Parents should not be put off taking an injured child to the doctor because of
the cost. Free after-hours visits for accident care will also enable families to seek the
urgent medical care they need when they need it.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What are the benefits of free after-hours accident care?
6126 Questions for Oral Answer 24 Oct 2012

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: ACC received claims fo r about 80,000 children aged
under 6 in the last year alone. Today’s a nnouncement will make a big difference for
those families who may have waited until the next day before seeing their general
practitioner. From December this year they  will no longer have to. Free after-hours
accident care visits will also help reduce the number of young children presenting at our
busy hospital emergency departments with an injury that a genera l practitioner could
have treated.
Hon John Banks—Compliance with Cabinet Manual
12. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
Has Hon John Banks satisfied the Cabinet Manual requirement of upholding the highest
ethical standards in his political and personal capacity?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How is John Banks’ refusal to release his witness statement to the
police upholding the standards of ministerial behaviour in  a personal and political
capacity?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know the particulars of  the case, but what I do know
about the Official Information Act is that the departments do have to cite relevant
sections of the Act if they choose to withhol d information. In the e nd, the decision to
release information is actually the responsib ility of the department—in this case, the
police.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Given his publicly stated commitment to high ministerial
standards, why will he not ask the Hon John Banks to allow his witn ess statement to be
released, or is that just a position of hypocrisy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The reason is that that was an action taken by Mr Banks, not
even in his capacity as the leader of the ACT Party but actually as a personal position.
He has the right, like any othe r New Zealand citizen, and if  the Labour Party wants to
go out there and publicly release the Darren Hughes file, we ll, it is welcome to do so as
well.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: If the Hon John Banks—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear this question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: If the Hon John Banks’ witness statement were  to show that he
had lied to him or his chief of staff, would he dismiss John Banks as a Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, that has always been the test, but the member is raising
a hypothetical question. I have be en assured by the member that  he has told us the truth
and I accept that as his word.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What would John Banks need to  do in order for him to lose
confidence in him as a Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: He would need to lose my confidence.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I move, That the
House take note of miscellaneous business . Last week I had the privilege to represent
the Government in India supporting and encouraging some wonderful New Zealand
companies and entrepreneurs and some of our excellent educational institutions that are
getting out there and selling their stuff, thei r innovation, and their Kiwi ingenuity to the
world. It was the same in the US a few weeks ago, and it was the same when I had the
opportunity to visit, aro und the country, regions like Hawke’s Bay, west Auckland,
Palmerston North, and so on.
It is not easy for these companies. It is hard work. These people live out of suitcases,
they get to know new markets, they deal with the heat, and they deal with the cold, but
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6127
it is also the thrill of the challenge and succeeding in this most 21st century of pursuits—
becoming successful in the global world. It is  also about creating things that people
value and then working with them to get th em to markets, partnering up with people,
obtaining capital, and making deals. It is challenging. We have always talked about
moving up the value chain, but we are doing it. The euro an d the US dollar are making
it challenging, but our companies are succeedin g. They are good at it, and organisations
that the New Zealand taxpayer supports, li ke New Zealand Trade and Enterprise,
Education New Zealand, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Tourism New
Zealand, and the research sector are all assi sting them in doing it. Our exports are up,
due to a lot of hard work from some great  Kiwi businesses, and jobs are growing. Our
economy has grown in the last 12 months faster than most countries in the OECD.
But meanwhile back home, the Labour, Greens, New Zealand First Opposition are in
a very dark space economically indeed. They are seeking to reintroduce 1970s-style
fortress New Zealand economics, last seen when  Mr Peters arrived in Parliament. They
want to somehow strong-arm down the Ne w Zealand dollar to decouple New Zealand
from the global world. Leaving aside that it does not work, and that it has not worked in
Switzerland and has not worked in Japan, and leaving aside that if it did work, it would
cause massive cost of living increases fo r all New Zealanders, and never mind the
depreciation of 20 percent of the New Zealand dollar as proposed by John Walley,
Selwyn Pellett, and other fello w travellers of the Labour Party, which would put up the
input costs of all New Zealand businesses, they want to go ahead and do it. They want
to control the New Zealand dollar and somehow decouple us from the world.
They also want to control and prevent fo reign investment in New Zealand. We had
the frankly preposterous suggestion from Mr Cunliffe last week that Ministers should
decide who owns Fisher and Pa ykel, not private shareholders. Well, if that actually was
allowed to pass, she’d be a very sorry day fo r capital investment in this country indeed.
In fact, we had a taste of that during th e last decade when the sharemarket went
sideways for all that time because of the strange policies of the previous Government.
They also want to halt immigration, ev en if it might help the rebuild in
Christchurch—halt immigration, even if it he lps the rebuild in Christchurch. They are
going to say to the people of Christchurch: “Well, it would be really great for us to build
these buildings, but we’re not going to bri ng anybody in from overseas to help do this.”
Two of New Zealand’s leading newspapers ha ve used the “x” word to describe that
policy. They have said xenophobia is what we are talking about with that policy.
Meanwhile their friends in the Greens are out there trying to stop every opportunity
to grow, with renewed vigour. They are opposed to oil exploration. They are opposed to
new mines. They are opposed to dairy farming. They are opposed to convention centres.
Together, imagine it: you would have the hapless Labour Party putting up the shutters to
stop New Zealand being involved in the world and hiding from the world and saying the
world is out there, but it is too scary; meanwhile, back at home you would have the
Greens stopping everything from happening, and Mr  Peters sitting ther e trying to work
out which way the weathervane will run on any particular day. We cannot nor should
we attempt to turn the clock back to the 1970s.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. Should he not be referring to
the Rt Hon Winston Peters? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have asked members not to interrupt 5-minute speeches.
The way the member was being referred to was not disrespectful. He referred to him as
Mr Peters. I think the member is technica lly absolutely correct , but I do not want 5-
minute speeches being interrupted like that . The Hon Steven Joyce has 14 seconds
remaining.
6128 General Debate 24 Oct 2012

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Fourteen seconds to go. We should not, nor can we attempt
to, turn back to the 1970s. Th ere is no mother England to  buy every mutton leg we can
grow. We live in a modern world. There ar e fantastic opportunitie s for New Zealand.
We need to help our country become more  competitive and suppor t the companies that
are getting out there and taking their chances and getting ahead.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I think that what has been
demonstrated before us in this Parliament today is a Government that does not
understand that the foundation of our econo my is our environment. We have a
Government that has launched a war on the New Zealand environment since it was re-
elected. The first term of this Government  was problematic enough, but to some degree
it was responsive to public opinion. The second term of this Government has launched a
war against the New Zealand environment,  and, hence, against the New Zealand
economy. Anyone who understands anythi ng about the New Zealand economy
understands that it is based on the environment.

items.speaker: The Prime Minister has said
items.text: “Well, we’re not environmental bandits.” Actually,
Government members have become envi ronmental bandits, under the influence
particularly of Mr Joyce, who does not s eem to understand that the environment is
important, and who is involve d in a war against it. The Oxford English Dictionary
describes a “bandit” as a lawless, desper ate marauder—something of a gangster. We
now seem to have a Cabinet th at is full of environmental bandits who are determined to
wage war on the environment. Let us look at climate change. This Government, in spite
of all the evidence showing that climate cha nge is accelerating and the Arctic ice cap is
melting more quickly, is weakening the emission s trading scheme to such a point that it
is completely useless. It is also very s upportive of digging up lignite and burning it, and
burning coal, which, of course, will accelerate climate change.
Let us look at the Ross Sea. This is a Government that has opposed attempts to
protect the Ross Sea. It could not even get alongside the proposal from the United
States, which was pretty modest. The proposal  from New Zealand was even worse than
the proposal from the United States, in terms of  protecting one of the last great pristine
seas.
Let us look at the M āui’s dolphin. There are only 55 M āui’s dolphins left. New
Zealand is very likely to be one of the c ountries to drive a dol phin to extinction, yet
repeatedly this Government has done ve ry little about it—vi rtually nothing. New
Zealand was the only country to vote agains t protection measures at the International
Union for Conservation of Nature confer ence. How embarrassing that that was New
Zealand’s legacy at that conference. We  voted against the protection of marine
mammals. When it comes to sea lions, this G overnment decided to allow 68 critically
endangered sea lions to be killed, rather than having a safer squid fishery. So the
Minister made a decision to kill 68 endangered sea lions, rather than protect them.
Let us look at deep-sea mining. We know  because of Deepwater Horizon, which
should have been a wake-up call for all of us, that there is no way to plug a hole at
2,000 metres under water, which is what th e Government is pr oposing to do. The only
thing that has worked overseas was a relief rig, which drilled a re lief well. That was
how they managed to solve the Deepwate r Horizon problem. This Government is
proposing to have deep-water drilling withou t relief rigs in place. That is grossly
irresponsible.
Then we have seen in respect of fresh water that this is a Government that is
subsidising the intensification of agricultu re, which will drive the deterioration in
freshwater quality. When we look overseas what  we see is that people overseas buy our
dairy products because they th ink New Zealand is clean, gr een, and safe. That is the
foundation of our export economy, and this Gove rnment is determined to destroy that
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6129
foundation with its attack on th e natural environment. This Government needs to get its
head in order, and realise that  if it is truly committed to th e long-term sustainability of
the New Zealand economy, it needs to become committed to the long-term
sustainability of the New Zealand environmen t, instead of waging a war on it. Whether
you look at climate change, whether you look  at what it is doi ng in the Ross Sea,
whether you look at the M āui’s dolphins, or whether you look at sea lions, deep-sea
mining, or fresh water—you could add to th e list one issue after another—since the
election, this Government has been attacking the environment.
My question is what is going on in Cabinet?  Once we thought that maybe there were
those in Cabinet who had some sympathy towards the environment—I guess we all
hoped Nick Smith would do that. But in the current Cabinet there are no advocates for
the New Zealand environment. All we have is decision after decision after decision
attacking the New Zealand environment, so th at future generations will inherit natural
capital that will be degraded  and, hence, undermine the long-term sustainability of our
economy. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The difference between us here on the
Government benches and those sitting on the othe r side in Opposition is clear. It is very
clear to us here in Parliament and it is very  clear to the people out  in our electorates.
That lot, the previous Labour Governme nt—and the Greens, w ho propped it up—had
the very best of times. It enjoyed the very be st of times. What did it do with all that
success? It spent it.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Squandered.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It squandered it—absolutel y. When Labour left office,
inflation was running at 5.1 pe rcent. The export sector was not talking about growth. In
fact, it was flatlining and it was struggling to survive. The back-office bureaucracy, the
media teams, the public relations consulta nts, the policy wonks, and the “Wassup!”
badge designers were all ballooning in numbers, and Treasury’s books showed decades
of deficits as government spending and debt  spiralled out of control. We were in
recession. We were in a recession, the like of which this country had not seen since the
1930s. That is 80 years ago.
But under careful and steady management, this Government has turned those
statistics round: steady increases in after-tax wages; inflation at 1 percent, not Labour’s
5 percent; mortgage rates at 5 percent, not Labour’s 11 pe rcent; a top personal tax rate
of 33 percent, not Labour’s 39  percent; and company tax at  28 percent, not Labour’s 30
percent. When Labour abolished the youth minimum wage in 2008, 9,000 young people
lost their jobs—9,000 young people. Yet the La bour Opposition brayed like asses when
we used dollars from Moroccan cooking clas ses for well-heeled adults to put extra
dollars into education and training fo r those very same young people whom that
previous Government had callously written out of employment.
The Taranaki region enjoys the highest region al growth in the count ry. It is the only
region that has oil and gas production and it has had that for 100 years. It has 4,500 jobs
directly involved in the oil and gas industry—4,500 jobs—and it has 1,500 jobs
indirectly involved. The average wage is $80,000 a year.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is $80,000. We envy Tarana ki. It is known for its dairy
industry, its tourism, and its oil and gas indus try. I come from the East Coast. We are
known for our sheep and beef farming, fore stry, horticulture and viticulture, and
tourism. Why can we not add oil and gas i ndustry to that list? Why can we not? Well,
this Government wants to.
Last week in the East Coast region just 64 jobs were notified to the Ministry of
Social Development—20 more than at this  time last year—but 3,637 job seekers were
6130 General Debate 24 Oct 2012
registered with the Ministry of Social Development in the region. Why would any of
those job seekers not want to work in the oil and gas industry as cooks, carriers, truck
drivers, plumbers, builders, or electricians, and maybe nurses, tea la dies, engineers, or
managers?
There are 763 youth job seekers registered wi th the Ministry of Social Development
in the East Coast region, down from 837 this  time last year. So a big thanks to the
schools, the tertiary providers, and the em ployers who have worked so hard for our
young people, but some of them will have le ft. Some of them will have gone to
Australia to get a job. So why cannot these young people work  in the East Coast, in
their own home town, in the oil and gas industry?
Well, Labour is all about saying no. Labour says no to everything that is proposed
that will provide those young people with jobs . Intensification of farming—Labour says
no. Australian companies moving jobs to New Zealand—Labour says no. Ninety-day
probation period for new employees—Labour  says no. The new youth starting-out
wage—Labour says no. To any of our labour market reforms, actually, Labour says no.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: If the Minister who has just resumed her
seat, the Minister of Police, wanted an idea as to how to retain Kiwis, the thousand a
week who are leaving our shores—including 17,000 Kiwi technicians, tradespeople, and
labourers—for Australia, she would do well to  look at a thing calle d the Christchurch
earthquake. We need 30,000 to 40,000 trade-trai ned, skilled people to rebuild the show.
It is one of the world’s bi ggest training schemes, on our  doorstep. We know that her
Government put forward a paltry 42 million bucks in trade training, 80 percent of which
is unused. We know that we have 84,000 young pe ople not in work and not in training.
This is a wonderful opportunity in Christ church, not only to reconstruct our second-
biggest city but also to deal with, and train, and get off the dole, 84,000 young people.
Yet what do we find out? We find out that th e latest reports are that we are going to
import 15,000—nearly half of the quota of trad e-trained people whom we need. We are
not going to train unemployed fo lk, as we could have done for the last 2 years. We are
going to import 15,000 of them because the Government lacked the foresight 2 years
ago to actually take those young people, train them, and turn them into productive
human beings. They would be 2 years through a 3 to 4-year apprenticeship. They would
have been highly skilled, hi ghly productive, and would ha ve aided and abetted the
rebuilding of Christchurch. So if the Minister wants to look for an opportunity—and she
is fond of quoting figures—she might look at the opportunity that the tragic earthquake
presents, instead of importing folk. It is  not xenophobic to say, as Gerry Brownlee
committed to, Cantabrians first, Kiwis second, and the rest of the world third, when it
comes to filling the capacity and the jobs that the earthquake has created. But, oh no.
The xenophobic label is put on by a few short- sighted in the media and that Minister
there.
We had a policy at the last election that wa s fiscally neutral. It  was about taking the
dole, giving it to the boss, the boss topping it up for 1 year, and the commitment is that
that young person be trained. You either use the dole to have the person languish, or
you give it to the boss for 1 year—same money, fiscally neutral. That is then turned into
a commitment to trade train that person, th rough a thing called an apprenticeship, and
allow that young person to contribute to the rebuild of Christchurch and take that person
off the dole. We put that to Gerry Brow nlee and others, and we reminded Gerry
Brownlee of the deal—Cantabria ns first, Kiwis second, the re st of the world, whom we
will need, last—and he did nothing about it.
I fondly remember the last time—I was not a member of Parliament—and I did
remind a former National Minister of Educa tion at the time, who I think did not have
the intellect, the smarts, or the capacity, when  that education Mini ster, I think in 1992,
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6131
repealed the 1983 Apprenticeship Act. The Mini ster did not have the intellectual rigour,
the smarts, or the capacity perhaps—maybe th at member does now—to realise the error
of his ways. But, of course, we have got past that, have we not? So I say to that Minister
over there that it might be time that she looke d at what is happening as a result of the
earthquake.
I went to a meeting of Ōuruhia School parents last night.  They are fabulous parents.
Their school is on the block. Apart from that, which my colleagues will deal with later,
these were great parents who want a future fo r their kids. They believed in the sort of
John Key brighter future. Some of them ha d teenagers who were looking for jobs and
looking for a future. Some of them, I wager,  are looking for trade training and want to
get out there and contribute. Bu t this Government does not ha ve the foresight, like its
predecessors, to take advantage of what is a tragedy, but al so an opportunity to take
those 84,000 young people, to trade train them , and to have them contribute in
Canterbury to that recovery process. Seve nteen thousand technicians and tradespeople
have gone to Aussie—a thousan d Kiwis a week—and that is the brighter future. Why
would you stay here? You would stay here  because there are opportunities, and the
Christchurch recovery gives that opportunity. Let us hope that this Government does not
repeat the stupidity of past National Ministers.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: That speech from Clayton Cosgrove
showed that he has learnt absolutely nothi ng from the rejection of him personally in
Waimakariri, and the rejection of the Labour Party’s whingeing negativity in
Christchurch. New Zealanders, and not just those in Canterbury, are looking for positive
leadership, which they are getting from this Government.
You see, the most important challenge for our country today is how we navigate our
way through the worst economic downturn si nce the Great Depression. This afternoon I
want to quote what President Obama’s budget o ffice adviser told the IMF last week. He
said “… if you look across all the develope d countries, there is only one country …
which has [the right policy combination] , which is New Zealand …”. What an
extraordinary compliment for the effective governance of this John Key - Bill English -
led Government, where in terms of economic policy we have ourselves in great shape.
Let me go through some of the vital signs of the New Zealand economy. Last week
we had the inflation figure: 0.8 percent. That is  the lowest level of inflation in 16 years.
What was the inflation rate when we came to Government? It was 5.1 percent. What
does that mean? That means ordinary New Z ealand families struggling to keep up with
the cost of groceries, with the cost of power bills, with the cost of their rates, and with
all of those things that make a difference for ordinary New Zealanders. On inflation
New Zealand is doing very, very well.
Let us take interest rates. Interest rates affect the capacity for businesses to invest and
to create jobs, and they impact on the costs of every single New Zealand family that is
aspiring for that Kiwi dream of being able to own their own home. The interest rate
right now is 5.3 percent. That is the lowest—the lowest—int erest rate in 40 years. And
how does it compare with the interest rate  when we became the Government? It was
over double that. It was at 11 percent. I know members opposite do not understand how
important low interest rates are to businesses and households. We do. It matters. We are
delivering.
Then let us look at a figure like economic  growth. What an extraordinary result,
given all that is going on globally, for the economy to have grown by 2.6 percent in the
last 12 months. I look around the world—Bri tain, Greece, Spain, Italy—extraordinary
economic collapse, extreme hardship, and millions of people going into unemployment.
Here in New Zealand we have had our economy growing for 13 straight quarters. Let us
just look back again to 2008. Do you know th at in 2008, in those three quarters of
6132 General Debate 24 Oct 2012
March, June, and October, it was not that we had economic growth; our economy had
negative growth and it was going backwards.
Let us look at one of the big issues: government debt. When we came into
Government, Treasury said we had a decade of deficits. The debt was going to blow out
to 70 percent of GDP, and yet, as was noted  at the IMF last week, New Zealand is one
of only three developed countries that is goi ng to have a balanced budget in the year
2015. I again give credit to Bill English and the team for being able to deliver that sort
of result.
I will mention another positive figure. Over  the last year New Zealanders’ debt
servicing costs have droppe d by $4 billion and New Zeal and households have saved
more in the last year than they have in 20 years. Every New Zealander knows at heart
that we need to improve our savings. That is an extraord inarily positive outcome. It is
just one of many vital signs that show that this Government is on top of its game and
that the economic management—the big issu e—we are getting right. I just challenge
members opposite to stop the negativity.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Interest rates in New Zealand
are four times that of the USA, the UK, th e EU, and Japan, and Nick Smith made that
claim! But, mind you, he made a claim that he advised Dame Margaret Bazley of a legal
fund when she was in charge of the parliame ntary pecuniary interests, except Margaret
Bazley denied it, and yet he wants to come  back and be a Minister when he told
Parliament something that was de monstrably not true. Look at the Hansard. It is all
there.
Yesterday, of course, the M āori Council won the right to take its case on State asset
sales and water rights to the High Court—just one tragic milestone along the road to
separate development, apartheid, and assets divided up on the basis of race. How, under
a National Party that campaigned on “Kiwi not iwi”—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It did, did it not? National campaigned on “Kiwi not
iwi”. How, therefore, has it come to this? What has New Zealand done to deserve this
appalling Government? What manner of Government is it that would plough on with its
misguided asset sales programme in the face of all the damage it is doing?
There is no sound economic rationale, and it gets worse. The whole process has been
botched, so inept and so shambolic that it is now further undermining New Zealand’s
social cohesion, and it is racism that the Government is encouraging. This very privative
campaign—inevitable to see that happen. A c ynical person might even suggest that this
Government intended to have that effect, as  people overlooked the nation’s interest and
scrambled for their share of the spoils. Why did the Government not foresee the discord
its sales programme would generate? It was spending $120 million on consultants to
give it advice. Surely, one consultant said that. So many trails and twists and no
coherence.
Does anyone remember “shares plus”? Well, last week it was iwi shares that were on
offer, coming out of nowhere. So now th e proceeds of the asset sales programme—
unquantified, of course—are going to pay o ff debt, pay for schools, pay for hospitals,
and now we learn out of left  field that they will also  be contributing to Treaty
settlements. How many times can the same m oney get spent? Where is this all going to
end? Who knows? Those members do not. They just blunder along—ad hoc, shoot from
the hip, chaotic, make it up as you go al ong—despite the serious damage that has been
inflicted on our country by this issue.
How petty and small-minded some peopl e are becoming, incl uding the Prime
Minister. In response to Rahui Katene of the M āori Council on the ques tion of the right
to go to court, this is what Mr Key said: “… hardly a victory when you get the judge to
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6133
agree to … your case.” So there you have it again: just “Spray and Walk Away”. A
classic Key one-liner—dismissive, flippant, sneering.
What is clear is that the issue will fester  and create future dispute and discord. How
many now think that the country is being held to ransom by certain M āori interests that
want to exploit the situati on to their own advantage? For those who want to undermine
our social cohesion, this Government’s asset sales programme has been a gift. It has put
Māori against other New Zealanders, M āori against Māori, and iwi against iwi. What a
mess. What a way to run a country. And what  a tragedy for New Zealand that someone
behind that court case is saying: “When th e water passes over our land or rohe, the
proprietorship right is with us.” Which pa rt of the water? The foundation, the middle
part, the end part, or whatever runs out to sea?
What a tragedy for New Zealand. But the polls say—and this is  the only good news
in this speech—that we will soon have to address this issue and set it to rights.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am very pleased to stand to
speak about economic growth and developmen t, particularly in the province that I
represent, which is Taranaki. I have hear d today, prior to coming to the House, a
statement that criticism is not an agenda. Th e more that that lot over the other side of
the House criticise, the more they have got nothing to say.
Last month I was invited to speak at a f unction in New Plymouth—the city in which
I live. It was hosted by a social justice group. An officer from the Ministry of Social
Development was one of the panellists, and he  informed the delegates that there were
280 people in the city of Ne w Plymouth who were receivi ng a benefit because they
were not employed—in a city of 50,000 people. If you look at Taranaki as a whole, with
a population of 110,000, unemployment in that  region has shrunk by 35 percent since
September 2010. Industry is flourishing, opportu nities are increasi ng, and employment
is growing. So while they say no, Taranaki is saying yes, and we are flourishing.
The biggest reason for Taranaki’s success is the responsible and act ive utilisation of
the resources that surround us. And those re sources are specifically, as you know, the
wealth that we walk on and the wealth that  is deeper under our feet. We utilise those
resources in responsible and careful ways.
New Zealanders are receiving the benefit of  a pro-business, pro-growth Government
that is not selling out on our environmental obligations. The exclusive economic zone
closes the environmental regulatory gap that existed while those on the other side of this
House did nothing when they were in a position to do something.
The oil and gas sector in Taranaki, as we have heard from the Hon Anne Tolley, is a
world-class industry applying cutting-edge  technology and proprietary intellectual
property. This has had an amazing flow-on effect not only into the industries and
businesses in the region but also into the wider community. That particular field of
endeavour and business is one of the corner stones of our economy.  It generates 17
percent of our GDP. More important, it contri butes to the capability and the capacity
within a number of industries that exist in our region. The expor ts that come—in 2009
$1.9 billion in export value from this indus try, and 17.5 million barre ls of oil—all of
these are facts, but they translate into j obs and into an envir onment of world-class
expertise, developing technology, and developi ng practices that maintain and protect
our environment.
One of the great things about Taranaki, if you have been there, Mr Speaker, and I am
sure you have, is the pristine environment in which we live, the clear air, and the
beautiful mountain streams—all of these things that we hol d in high value. I know that
many members of this House have been there. So it is in our interests and, of course, the
interests of all New Zealanders that we maintain all of those environmental standards
that have come to deliver a great province and a great environment for us.
6134 General Debate 24 Oct 2012
I have to say that it is nearly laughable that members of the Green Party try to poke
and jab the industry in Taranaki and the regul ators of that industry, and all the time are
trying to throw spanners in the works to say that what is happening is below par. If you
have ever read in the papers that come  from our region the accusation and then the
response from the regulators, it is actually poetry in motion. If Mr Hughes, in particular,
were to go there, he would try to throw his spin ball, and the Taranaki Regional
Council, in particular, the regulators ther e, have answers for every one of his
accusations and his allegations of impropr iety. We have a tremendous group of
regulators there. Recently we heard that we have had some responses from the Taranaki
Regional Council that indeed stand up to its great credibility.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Ngā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia ora. I want to touch on
the theme raised by my colleague Dr Russel Norman on the extreme anti-environment
ideology we are seeing from the National Party this term in Government. I want to look
at just one example, which is the Ross Sea, because here we have environmental bandits
in Cabinet literally acting not in our interest and ac tively damaging our economic
interest, our environmental interest, and our  community interest. They say they care
about the environment like the Ross Sea, but what we know is the way they are acting—
the way they are acting like environmental bandits—is akin to a hypocritical fashion.
The Ross Sea, or the last ocean, as it is known, is the last intact marine ecosystem
left on Earth. This beautiful wild  place is described by the journal Science as the place
least impacted by human hand on the planet. Unlike most places on the planet, the top
predator is still there. This is the last ocean because it is the last place where man’s
impact is being felt, but it is also the la st place we are going on our relentless push to
catch more fish. But we have an opportunity to change it, to protect it, because right
now in Hobart the Commission for the Convention on Antarctic Marine Living
Resources is meeting to discuss how we protect all the waters in Antarctica, but this, for
New Zealand, is the most precious part, what has been described as the last ocean.
What we have, however, is that after more  than a year of negotiations on a joint
proposal with the United States Government, we see those bandits in Cabinet urging the
Minister of Foreign Affairs to walk out of the joint US  proposal, and now New Zealand
has tabled its own proposal. It is a proposal in which McCully has literally drawn a line
round the main fishing grounds and created a marine reserve only on paper. It is a
marine reserve where the areas where we do not impact—where we do not exploit—are
left entirely within the marine reserve, but  those areas where we do exploit are left out.
It looks big on paper—it is a paper sanctuar y—but what it lacks in  effectiveness it
makes up for and compensates in size.
Basically what we see is those bandits in Cabinet protecting the fishing interests, not
protecting this pristine, beautiful place, the last ocean. We see the Government
swallowing hook, line, and sinker  the spin we see from th e fishing industry. What we
know is that we are protecting very narrow fishing interests—a handful of fishing boats,
some contracted to other nations. We are ta lking about 0.17 percent, or a fifth of 1
percent, as the catch landed in the Ross Sea by New Zealand boats, compared with our
larger catch. We are talking about around 1 percent of our fisheries exports, but what we
are doing is damaging our brand. By looking out for protecting these narrow fishing
interests we are actually letting down all of our fishing exports.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: From Shane Jones.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Mr Young, we are letting down a ll $1.5 billion of our fishing
exports. We know already that US supe rmarkets like Safeway are boycotting New
Zealand - caught Ross Sea toothfish.
It is bizarre that we woul d even walk out of a join t US proposal. I thought this
Government would want to go the Commi ssion for the Convention on Antarctic Marine
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6135
Living Resources with a joint New Zealand proposal. It is one of our aims to work
closer with the United States Gove rnment, if you look at the New Zealand
Government’s spin. What we know is that we are also damaging the chance of an
outcome now that we have got three proposal s on the table: the New Zealand weak one,
the US proposal, and also the better Antarctic Ocean Alliance.
But I want to clear up one thing. What we  know is—not the extremism we hear from
members like Shane Jones—none of those three proposals is going to ban fishing. None
of those three proposals is reducing the toothfish quota.
The fact is that New Zealand once upon a tim e was a world leader in protecting the
continent, the land and the ice of Antarctica, but we are failing to protect our oceans.
The Government describes it as a well-m anaged fishery. Well, it might be in
comparison to our poorly managed fisheries around New Zealand waters or what we see
in other countries, but the fact is that we still know so little about this toothfish, yet we
want to remove an entire 50 percent of its population. We s till have not found a
toothfish egg, larvae, or an under 4-year-old juvenile. This  place is under ice for 9
months of the year. We just do not have accurate information to make these decisions.
We have to ask ourselves why we are going to the ends of the world to catch the fish.
What happened to the rest of th e fish that was in all the wo rld’s oceans? The fact is we
have eaten them. We have eaten the fish a nd now we have to go right to the limits of
endurance technology, to the frontiers of the world, to the last ocean.
The Government says we are down there to protect it from pirates. The same
argument was used in England in the age of the slavery debates—that they should keep
participating in an improper practice to help  somewhat improve the standards. If that
was the argument, why are we not going to So malia? The fact is that if we were going
to reduce piracy, the best way we could do it is by having no fishing boats down there
so that we would know where the fishermen are.
The fact is that Labour does not have a position, it has got only slogans. The
Government is out there protecting fishing interests. We can protect the last ocean.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tena koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātou e te Whare. I wanted to take  an opportunity to talk on the k ōhanga reo report
released earlier this week. I f eel a bit of a hypocri te doing so in English rather than
Māori, bearing in mind the relationship between kōhanga reo and Te Reo Māori, but, be
that as it may, I let that sit here.
The survival and the strength of Te Reo M āori has been an issue at the forefront of
decades of devotion and advo cacy—protest after protest, h īkoi after h īkoi, submission
after submission, report after report. In the 1986 report on Te Reo Māori claim, and then
in the 2011 Ko Aotearoa T ēnei report on the Wai 262 claim, we were warned that the
likelihood of the terminal decline threat ening the very survival of Te Reo M āori was
imminent. In speaking to the Wait angi Tribunal in 1985, Sir James H ēnare cast the
Māori language predicament in stark terms. What  he said was: “Ko te reo te mauri o te
mana Māori.”—the language is the life force of the mana M āori. He continued: “If the
language dies, as some predict, what do we have left to us? Then, I ask our people who
are we?”.
Those are pretty important statements—provocative statements, some might suggest.
The founders of the kaupapa k ōhanga reo responded to th at challenge, creating a
movement that was never intended to be a bout only early childhood education but also
encompassed te reo Māori, tikanga Māori, and, of course, whānau development.
Last week the tribunal stat ed that without Te Reo M āori me ng ā tikanga M āori,
Māori would not survive, and that the two are basically inextricably linked. The
Waitangi Tribunal has now conf irmed that the trust’s clai m was well founded, that the
Crown has breached the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, and that kōhanga reo have
6136 General Debate 24 Oct 2012
suffered severe prejudice as a result of th e actions of the Crown and omissions by the
Crown. It went on further to suggest that unless k ōhanga reo are supported and specific
enrolment targets are achieved, Te Reo M āori will indeed die. We are talking about
something pretty serious, and therefore we hope that the report will be taken seriously.
Although the tribunal recommendations and findings are not binding on the Crown—
that is another debate, and it has been rais ed on a number of occasions—the report does
put on record the problems that the kōhanga reo and the trust have encountered, and lays
the foundation for setting things right into the future. The Crown is now on notice that it
must take especially vigorous action to protect Te Reo Māori through kōhanga reo. That
is the challenge that the M āori Party is prepared also to  keep a watching brief on, to
ensure that something does come out of that report.
I want to encourage all members of  this House to read the report Matua Rautia for
the excellent history it provides of the uni que and, indeed, inte rnationally renowned
impact of the k ōhanga reo movement. It traces back in time to the days of Kara
Puketapu from here, the successes of the T ū Tangata scheme, and the 1979 hui
kaumātua held at Waiwhet ū, where it was agreed that urge nt action was needed to take
control of the future destiny of the language  and to plan for its survival. Out of te
Wānanga Whakatauira in 1981 was establishe d a working party chaired by Sir James
Hēnare and comprising, amongst others, Lady Tilly Reedy, Ruka Broughton, Sir Mōnita
Delamere, and Archdeacon K īngi Īhaka, some of whom have now passed away. Out of
this group emerged the origins of the kōhanga reo strategy.
If I could just read how Dame Iritana T āwhiwhirangi described it, she said: “Dr
Tamate Reedy, Deputy Secretary at the time, then came up with the idea of full
immersion. The idea was that the language shou ld be learned in the same way a child
learns a language, in the context of a ho me environment. Thus the concept that
developed was that the language should be ‘caught’ rather than ‘taught’ in those early
years.” The rest, of course, is history. It is our history.
The tribunal challenges us, then, to consider that wh ānau have the right to choose
kōhanga reo as a viable path, a cultural pa th to preserve and promote Te Reo M āori me
ngā tikanga. It asks the Crown to reprioritise spending on Te Reo M āori and to provide
urgent funding for property maintenance and upgrades, to avoid e xposing, it says, the
3,000 mokopuna tamariki to the possibility of losing their buildings. The report reminds
us that the Crown cannot put in regulations  that are one-size-fits-all, and that k ōhanga
reo should not be assessed by the Educatio n Review Office in a way that undermines
the kaupapa. It encourages the Crown to promote and uphold the policy in a way that
will respect the kaupapa and allow k ōhanga reo to flourish. We hope that that is what
the Crown actually does.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: Ministers and former Ministers have
sat opposite today and kidded th emselves that they are doi ng a good job. What we are
here talking about today is oppor tunity lost, particularly oppor tunity lost in relation to
jobs, to skills, and to educa tion, and particularly in relation to the opportunity that
Christchurch afforded us.
The Government’s 2011 Budget—a pre-electi on Budget, when the Government was
full of verve and wanting to court the vote— talked about Christchurch, the rebuild, and
the opportunity that was afforded there. Mi nister Joyce told us : “The government is
committed to ensuring that people in Canterbury have the chance to build their skills, so
they can contribute to the rebuild of their city. This extra funding will ensure they have
that opportunity,”. Well, that has been a monumental fail.
Let me take you through that 2011 Budge t package, and let me tell you about
opportunity lost, a Government that lacks vision, and a Government that is failing its
people. It was heralded that $42 million of  extra funding was allocated to train our
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6137
young people with the skills needed to rebuild  Christchurch. We were going to train
them up. Well, what has happened? This is a Government that has managed to spend
only $8 million of that money. It has mana ged to train only 654 people with that
money—

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: —654 of our young people, of the 84,000 young New
Zealanders not in education, employment, or  training. This is a Government that has
managed to shift only 654 of them, despite having money in the Budget. Instead, what
has it done? It has cribbed $28.4 million from other places in the tertiary education
budget. It was meant to do this to create 3,000 places using baseline funding, but it has
failed even in this. It has managed only 1,626 placements within this. It has failed on
this, and it has failed to deliver.
Not only did Budget 2011 promise training opportunities in terms of the Skills for
Canterbury package but it also promised th at it was going to get our young people off
the dole, into work, and into training. The Government—pre-election and courting the
vote—accordingly allocated $1.5 million to shift 650 of our young people off the dole
and into education and training. Well, that  is a failure—yet another failure by this
Government. It has managed to spend only $740,000, less than half  of its allocated
money.
But more abysmally, and where it is faili ng our young people, is that it has managed
to shift only 262 people from the dole and into  work or training associated with the
rebuild of Canterbury. It has not met its  targets, and it is failing our young people.
Meanwhile, 84,000 of our young New Zealande rs continue to languish, not in
education, employment, or training. We ar e still waiting for the opportunities. We are
still waiting for the Government to actually come up with and do something meaningful
to address this problem of 84,000 of our young people.
Christchurch offers the Government that opportunity, and we are disappointed that it
is not taking that opportunity. We are still waiting for the Government to actually do
something in terms of the infrastructure rebuild of Canterbury. On the day that it
announced its “firm proposals” for the closur e of Christchurch schools, it was also
meant to be launching an employment package around the Stronger Christchurch
Infrastructure Rebuild Team and the infrastructure rebuild, but this has disappeared, and
we on this side of the House would like to know where it is.
In terms of the relationships  with industry, there is just  a whole lot of  talk—all good
in theory, but a failure. The much-vaunted re lationships with industry—well, let me tell
you. The relationship with Hawkins Cons truction has resulted in 75 young people
getting into training or employment—75—and 26 with Fletcher Building. That is not
good enough. This is a Governme nt that needs to  do something about offering real
opportunity to our young people.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I am very proud to be a member of
this John Key - led Government. I think we have a shared vision and a plan to support
New Zealanders through these troubled ec onomic times. We believe in helping New
Zealanders make the best of their opportunities. We recognise person al responsibilities,
and we also believe very strongly that peopl e need to be rewarded for their hard work
and their enterprise. These are values that  I believe in, and these are values that
underpin what is driving our plan to help  the New Zealand economy. Let us look at
some of the business investment initiatives that lead to new jobs—specific measures,
including the 90-day trial period and reduci ng company tax to 28 percent. We have
reduced ACC levies and saved $600 million a year with that measure alone. We have
also removed 170 unnecessary and excessive re gulations because we are not about red
tape. We are not about binding up business and holding back the economy, unlike the
6138 General Debate 24 Oct 2012
Opposition. Most of these measures are completely lost on the Opposition. Those
members have had their crack at it and they have failed dismally. We are not about to be
sidetracked or distracted by the braying of the opposing forces.
I think that one of the things that has work ed most successfully in the past year has
been the efforts that we have made—and the Hon Paula Bennett in particular is to be
congratulated on this—in getting people off benefits and back into work. That is vital. It
is vital for themselves, for their self-esteem and their mana, and also for the future of
their family economy and the wider economy as well. These are vital things. What have
we done to help people back into work, pa rticularly our young people? What have we
done specifically? In the Youth Opportuni ties package alone there is $152 million,
which includes 4,000 places in Job Ops. In the past 2 years, in net terms, something like
60,000 more New Zealanders have been put into work. Our unemployment forecast is
definitely forecast to fall. This has all b een possible because the economy has grown. It
has grown by 2.6 percent in the year to June . Our annual growth forecast is between 2
percent and 3 percent over the next 4 years.  That is a lot better than other developed
countries are doing at the moment. The after-t ax average wage is up by 20 percent from
when Labour’s time ended in 2008. We now have—and this is a particularly good
thing—the lowest inflation rate since 1999, which means that the cost of living is
increasing at its lowest rate in 12 years. This is all good, and this is going to support
jobs.
But we are certainly not leaving it to chance, nor are we going into loopy, mad Green
ideas à la Zimbabwe to print money and shut  down opportunities fo r jobs and stall the
economy. If printing money was the recipe, then that country would be successful. It is
not. Printing money increases the money suppl y, so that increases inflation. It would
make the very people whom the Opposition is purporting to help suffer more difficulty
because everything would go up in price, from  the price of petrol to the price of
groceries. The poor would be the hardest hit. But the Greens and Labour are determined
to talk New Zealand down, and to promote a bunch of ideas that are in vogue only in the
sorts of countries that have run out of all other options.
We have not run out of options. We have a plan and we are sticking to it. As I have
said in the past in this sort of situation, st anding up in a general debate, it is a very good
plan and I support it because economic growth  produces jobs, and that is what we are
allowing to happen. But do not just take our word for it. Peter Orzag—as my colleague
the Hon Nick Smith referred to recently in his call today—has singled out New Zealand
as the only country that has provided the right balance of  stimulus for the economy, by
reducing the deficit in the medium term. This  is high praise indeed from someone who
has been looking carefully at our measures a nd looking carefully at wh at we are able to
do.
I think when it comes to New Zealand’s ec onomic performance, for me on the North
Shore I look at what has happened with in frastructure and with the broadband rolling
out. I can see that people in my area, in my electorate of North Shore, are delighted with
that. I was just looking for so me tangible information that I had about this because I
have had several letters from my constituents about the growing of the economy, and in
particular how the broadband has helped. In days gone by, when North Shore Hospital
was not in such fettle, there were real issu es about people in corridors and people not
getting the level of care that  they required. With the br oadband roll-out, it is now
possible to upload and send a file of a sick child within 3 seconds to Starship. These are
the kinds of measures that are making a phen omenal difference. That is why in these
tough economic times we are continuing to invest in them.
As far as the Opposition is concerned, though, it would want to borrow to pay for
reducing things like the retirement age. It wants to lower it to 60 years old for many
24 Oct 2012 General Debate 6139
workers. What is that going to do? Borrowing again to pay for the Auckland rail loop—
failed policies.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I want to begin by
acknowledging that families in Christchurch  have been through an emotional roller
coaster since they struggled to get to the schools where their children were on 22
February last year. I want to acknowledge all of those teachers and principals who stood
alongside those children until their parents c ould make it there. They guaranteed the
children one thing for those parents: they would be kept safe and sound until they
arrived at the school. Of course , it is the memory of that care and, indeed, the memory
of how well the schools have provided both a stable environment and a sense of
normality for these children that has left the communities with a sense of absolute
obligation and respect for the teachers and fo r the schools, in terms of how they have
supported their communities. That is why th ese communities are ab solutely despairing
of the Minister of Education’s shake-up in education.
We have already debated in the House how  this was handled by the Government. It
was appalling. There could be no worse way of actually diminishing the respect for both
the schools and the situation in Christch urch, with people suffering from the ongoing
effect of aftershocks, even minor ones—I th ink one last night woke people up again. It
is just a constant reminder of the difficulti es that people face. Then we ended up with
this sudden announcement. With the impact on principals and boards of trustees who
were brought to a meeting, with no idea what  was about to be announced, and the way
they were treated, how their schools found out, and then how their communities found
out, it really has been  the worst handled of all of th e earthquake-related announcements
that this Government has been  responsible for, and it ha s been responsible for some
pretty serious ones.
This is not how one empowers communities after a disempowering event. Sir Peter
Gluckman, who writes as the Chief Science Advisor for the Prime Minister, said this is
not the way that one ensures that communities can recover from the consequences of the
disaster. We have got a man-made disaster on our own hands now as a result of the way
the Government is treating the response to education.
But I do want to acknowledge that the Minister, according to the  Press this morning,
has written to the 38 schools th at are now earmarked for clos ure or merger to say, at
last, that she will want to talk to them, that  she would like to hear from them, and that
she will listen to them. I want  to hold her to that account. I will be holding her to that
account, as will every member of the Opposition in this House, because it is absolutely
imperative that she restores the damage th at she has done by fixing the problem. Those
schools that have asked for an extension of time must be granted an extension of time. It
should not be a question of whether they can persuade her or not, or that she will just
consider it, as she said in the House yesterda y; she must agree to the extension of time.
It is simply untenable that schools a nd their communities that struggle under the
circumstances in Christchurch have got term  4 to respond to the proposal to close or
merge their schools. That is 7 December this year. That simply is not good enough.
The schools I have talked to have asked for an extension to the end of term 1, which
is April 2013. That says to me that the sc hools are reasonable. They are willing and
reasonable to listen to the Minister’s call for change. In fact, they want to see change.
They know that things cannot go back to th e way they were. But when I read in the
paper that at the same time she said that she understood how difficult the changes were
for Christchurch, but given the extent of the damage and the population movement the
sector simply could not be returned to how it wa s, I just want to say that that adds insult
to injury.
6140 General Debate 24 Oct 2012
Every single school is willing to have the c onversation about the future of education.
They have shown willing in terms of the care and support they have given those
children in difficult circumstances. They want to build back better. They want to make
sure that they are responsive to the needs of their community. That is why they all
engaged openly in the conversation around the education recovery plan. The previous
Minister of Education made it absolutely clea r that that process was not about places or
services; it was about the principles of what education could provide and would provide
for the future of Christchurch. And yet we have suddenly had it tu rned into specific
places and services. We have had specific options determined by the Minister, and I
want to say that there is no way on earth that a Labour Gove rnment would allow that to
happen.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
In Committee
Debate resumed from 23 October.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Could I express my gratitude and that of my party to the
Government and to other parties in the House for the change to the rules of engagement
for this part to enable us to take an adequate number of calls.
I have spoken several times in the Chamber about the Ottawa Charter in this debate,
and in particular about the sense in the O ttawa Charter, to wh ich New Zealand is a
signatory, that to improve the health of  a community we need to empower that
community—I will deal with that part of the charter in another call—but also to create a
supportive environment around that comm unity. The evidence that the Law
Commission heard and that members of this  Committee are, I think, all too familiar
with is that the environmen t that some of our most marginalised and vulnerable
communities are surrounded by is such that they  are practically being basted in alcohol.
It is impossible for them to escape the ubi quity of alcohol outlets  and sales if they
choose to.
Essentially, in recent years we have come to a situation where alcohol is available for
sale in pretty much every community in the country, essentially 24/7—24 hours a day, 7
days a week. Indeed, there are around 1,000 outle ts in New Zealand that are licensed to
sell alcohol on a 24/7 basis. Indeed, in the years between 1990 and 2010, in that 20-year
period, there has been an addition—an explos ion—of 8,000 new outlets selling alcohol.
Certainly, members will be aware of many alcohol outlets in our own communities.
These new outlets are not randomly distri buted throughout the c ountry or throughout
communities or population centres, but, rath er, are clustered in low socio-economic
status areas. They are clustered in the areas inhabited by the most vulnerable and
marginalised. The distance that a person would need to travel in a low socio-economic
status area, on average, to make it to an  alcohol outlet is 50 percent less than the
equivalent high socio-economic status suburb or area. It is ju st an indication of how the
24 Oct 2012 Alcohol Reform Bill 6141
alcohol industry, at its vari ous levels, has targeted thes e low socio-economic status
communities.
The effects of this are considerable. Th e evidence is, and I quote from the Drug
Foundation again, that “For every off-licence, within a kilometre of a residential area,
there is a 4 percent increase in binge dri nking. Outlet density is linked to underage
drinking, student drinking, and high-risk drinking by young people.” The weight of
evidence is that when the density of alcohol  outlets increases, we  also see increased
rates of violence and physical assaults, sexually transmitted infections, child abuse,
drink-driving, and those other deleterious consequences of alcohol consumption or
heavy alcohol consumption that this bill, the Alcohol Reform Bill, sets out to minimise.
So there is a direct relationship between ou tlet density and the purpose of this bill,
which is to minimise harm.
I mentioned yesterday that 70 percent of our presentations to accident and emergency
departments over weekends are from people who have been consuming alcohol, and I
talked about those 1,000 d eaths per year. Those are some of those negative
consequences associated with the outlet densit y. There are also aspects of availability
that relate to the hours that these outlets  are open. Indeed, there is strong evidence
showing that longer trading hours mean increas ed negative and harmful effects. I will
not go through that list again, but it is clear that  both outlet density and increased outlet
hours are associated with increased harm. So if we want to deal with that harm—and
this bill says that we do want to deal with it—then we need to address both of those
factors.
In the way that the bill sets out to do that , I think there are some advances, but those
advances, as with every other part of th e bill, do not go far enough. Again, the Green
Party will be voting for all of the Supplem entary Order Papers that have been put
forward by Opposition members and by the M āori Party to actually gain greater control
over where outlets are and the hou rs that they can be open in order to minimise that
harm. The evidence around support for those measures is strong. As usual, the scientific
research around those factors says that thes e are very effective means of limiting harm,
and the Law Commission, indeed, drew some conclusions that were stronger than those
in the bill itself.
But it is not only the Law Commission. The Ne w Zealand public has also had its say
through the Health Sponsorship Council survey in 2010, which showed that 66 percent
agreed or strongly agreed with reducing the hours that alcohol can be sold. In addition
to that 66 percent, there were a further 18 percent who were neutra l about that point.
That is a vast majority who are either suppor tive of our tackling that issue or are neutral
about it. There were 65 percent of New Z ealanders who thought there were too many
liquor outlets. I am going to come in a later call to the issue of local alcohol policies, but
for the time being what I want to emphasise is the importance of taking this measure.
Again, just as with the calls we heard earli er in this Committee stage, we are dealing
here with an issue that  there is strong evidence around, a nd I will be very  interested to
hear the Minister of Justic e’s calls and other calls take n by Government members to
defend the course that is set out in the bill, wh ich I consider to be inadequate. This is in
contrast to the raging debate that we had around purchase age only a short time ago,
where there is very little evidence indeed of  effectiveness. Here is something that has
strong evidence of effectiveness, that is recommended by the Law Commission, and
that enjoys a very high level of support fr om the New Zealand public. We believe that
the bill sets out in the right direction, but does not go nearly far enough. We want to see
much more control over where outlets can be. Louisa Wall’s amendments around
schools, for example, are a good example of the kind of restriction that we would like to
see in general applied right across the c ountry, in addition to the locally specific
6142 Alcohol Reform Bill 24 Oct 2012
controls that local alcohol policies will produc e. And we want to see a very substantial
restriction of the hours that alcohol can be  sold. We heard yesterday from Trevor
Mallard in this debate a contribution wher e he opposed, on the basis of his personal
experience, the idea of restricting the hours of sale of alcohol.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s right—shift workers. Stand up for the shift workers.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Indeed. I have been a shift worker myself and have always
somehow managed to get a drink.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): Malo le soifua, Mr Chairman. Thank
you for the opportunity. I want to address my  remarks to Part 3, Subpart 3 of the
Alcohol Reform Bill, and more particularly the amendment that is in my name, on
Supplementary Order Paper 111. But I want to begin with some preliminary comments.
If people look at South Auckland, they will fi nd that in the past several years that
community has been under constant attack on several fronts, which has had significant
impact on people’s well-being in the areas of high unemployment, the high deficit in
housing affordability, the low wages, and the area  of health. In health we have some of
the worst statistics—worse than other comm unities throughout Aotearoa. In that area,
alcohol, particularly  alcohol-fuelled viol ence, alcohol-fuelle d domestic violence,
alcohol-fuelled suicide, and alcohol-fuelled mu rders, as we all know, have been in the
papers of late and in the past  several years. We often forget that this is really about a
portion of the community that abuses the co nsumption of alcohol, but that over the
years it has been a part of a culture that collectively we have built up.
In South Auckland, we are beset with the pr oliferation of liquor outlets, more so in
our community than in other communities. We  have got signs of alcohol advertising
that litter our streets, giving full exposu re to everybody, particularly young people who
are walking to and from school. We have he ard in the news of deaths of young people
who have either, essentially, abused the consumption of alcohol or committed suicide,
fuelled by the culture that it is OK to get wasted. We continue as a country to perpetuate
the alcohol culture—that it is OK to get drunk, it is OK to get wasted. The South
Auckland communities, I have to say, are sick and tired of that. You, Mr Chair, and my
colleague here, Louisa Wall, will know full well that over the past several years there
have been marches, there have been protes ts, and there have been community meetings
held, and you will find that th ere is a unanimous feel in th e community that we are sick
and tired of the alcohol culture, which ma ny of our community be lieve is driven by
vested interests that are contrary to the in terests of children and families. The majority
of communities want parliament arians to take seriously the recommendations of the
Law Commission.
Our front-line emergency people at Middlemore Hospital are sick and tired of having
to deal with fixing the broken bones, the wounds , etc., that come in  the early hours of
the morning. The police themselves have said  that they want parliamentarians to
toughen up on alcohol availability to protect our communities. I have to say that, by and
large, you will find that in the commun ity in South Auckland there is great
disappointment that when they had hoped that we had this opportunity as the
Government, as parliamentarians, to really  make a change for the better for the
community, that has not been the signal th at this Government has given to our
community.
So I want to introduce a Supplementary Orde r Paper. I will be looking to support all
the other Supplementary Order Papers that colleagues are putting forward, because I
think it is an opportunity that we should not  miss to make some changes that will
support our communities and protect future ge nerations from a culture that we have
contributed to over the years. My Supplem entary Order Paper proposes an amendment
to the Alcohol Reform Bill to provide an opportunity for schools’ boards of trustees and
24 Oct 2012 Alcohol Reform Bill 6143
early childhood centres within a radius of 3 kilometres to have their views taken into
account when an application for a liquor licen ce is made in that area. The amendment
provides an opportunity for schools and early  childhood education centres, if they so
choose, to have a say in the location of liquor outlets, with a view to reducing children’s
exposure to alcohol on their way to a nd from school. We ha ve too many in my
community, and almost all of these outlets w ill have huge signs, as I have said, that
litter our streets and place themselves in the face of children on the way to and from
school.
I think most of us will agree that you will find that most of the community
representatives on the school boards of trustees or earl y childhood education centres
will have a better idea than most and pr ovide accurate information on which liquor
outlets have behaved respons ibly in their ar eas, and which outle ts blatantly act
irresponsibly and flout the law in adve rtising, selling to under-age children, and
allowing drinking outside their premises. Ther e is general consensus that the harm in
the communities is caused by not only t hose intoxicated or who abuse alcohol
consumption but also by those who sell liquor in an ir responsible manner. For the
communities who care about what happens in their neighbourhoods, especially with the
children in our communiti es, there is a strong feeling that  we have got to do all we can
to at least limit the harm and abuse that aris e from alcohol availability, and in particular
the exposure of young children to alcohol.
My Supplementary Order Paper provides an opportunity to the members of the local
community boards of trustees of schools or early childhood centres to have their say and
be heard if they choose to provide a view on the location of li quor outlets in their
communities. The Minister of Justice, I understand, has pointed out that the Alcohol
Reform Bill has provisions for local alcohol  policy to be established, and she has
indicated that, therefore, she will not suppor t my Supplementary Order Paper. I would
say that although the Alcohol Reform Bill doe s provide for local alcohol policy, these
provisions are voluntary, and unl ess the council initiates it those local alcohol policies
will not exist. Furthermore, the process for es tablishing local alcohol policies will be a
long public consultative pro cess, which we all know can be quite draining on the
community and can certainly be quite expens ive. My amendment offers an alternative
that can happen immediately, without the drawn-out consultative process, and can
eliminate the costly normal public process. And though it might be difficult for the
boards of trustees to be able to determine the future impact of any alcohol availability
and advertising on children, my amendment at least provides an opportunity for the
local community to be heard if it so choos es, and for the district  licensing agency to
consider the concerns of that community and of that school, and th e substance of those
concerns.
I would urge members of the Government, b ecause it is up to them in terms of the
numbers, not only to support my amendment but, I think, to take seriously all the
amendments that members have put up. It is not about politicking; it is about genuinely
representing the strong views that do exis t. And the Minister will know this, because
those views also exist in her community, in Papakura. So I move that. Thank you.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. Thank you very much
for the opportunity to contribute to the debate. My Supplementary Order Paper 107
really wants to put children at the heart of policy. My community of Manurewa has over
30 off-licence liquor outlets, bu t within the context of th e greater Manukau—and it is
great that I have followed on from my colleague Su’a William Sio—we have 494 liquor
licences. We have 181 off-licence facilities. Unfortunately for our community, we fit a
lot of the profile that my colleague Kevi n Hague was talking about. In terms of the
demography of my electorate, we have 14 decile 1 schools, we have nine decile 2
6144 Alcohol Reform Bill 24 Oct 2012
schools, and we have four decile 3 schools. So of the 29 schools in my electorate, 27 are
either decile 1, decile 2, or decile 3. That really is at the hear t of my Supplementary
Order Paper, which is about enabling commun ities to self-regulate, but from a clean
slate.
The reason my Supplementary Order Pape r came to be was that just before
Christmas the Myers Road superette appl ied for a liquor licence. The Myers Road
superette lies between two schools, Ma nurewa East School and Greenmeadows
Intermediate School. The communities were so enraged by the fact that there was an
application for a liquor licence that they leafleted all the homes in the suburb, which is
part of the Manurewa electorate, and we ha d 400 submissions from members of that
community opposing that liquor application. I want to take this opportunity to commend
the leadership of Phil Palfrey, the princi pal of Manurewa East, Cathy Chalmers, the
principal of Greenmeadows Intermediate School, and also Colleen Brown, a member of
the Manurewa Local Board, who holds the portfolio of alcohol.
For us it was an opportunity to mobilise th e community, which actually did not need
much motivation to get mobilised in terms of writing a submission. They had 20 days. I
guess the process for us was won because, wh en the application was made, there was a
try to subvert the opportunity for our Manurew a community to have a say in the issuing
of that licence for that superette to sell alcohol.
The experience of our community has been that communities can make a difference,
and that communities want to ensure that our children grow up in an environment where
they can grow and develop in a positive wa y. So the Supplementary Order Paper about
banning off-licence premises within 1 kilometr e of a school is very much a recognition
that our schools are our learning, nurturi ng centres for our children and that the
immediate environment around our schools needs to be protected.
Where did the 1 kilometre limit come from ? Actually, I wanted it to be a bit
further—3 kilometres would have been good—but  the reality is that children who live
within a kilometre of school actually walk  to school. My contention—and, I am sure,
the contention of the House—is that alcohol is a product that shou ld be consumed by
adults only. There is no place in the life of a child for alcohol, and what really concerns
me is that our children who do walk to sc hool and stop at the lo cal superette on their
way to school are going to be confronted w ith alcohol in their environment, normalised.
We are going to have kids who are going to  be buying fruit, pies  probably too, and
